correctness.rationale: After width normalization, reducedness supplies primitive width directions uniquely selecting adjacent vertices. If those directions generated a proper sublattice, a nonzero lattice point (or its complement in the fundamental parallelogram) would lie in the triangle spanned with the origin and hence in the interior of the polar, contradicting normalized lattice width; therefore they form a lattice basis. The resulting normal form is \(\operatorname{conv}\{\pm(1,r),\pm(-s,1)\}\), \(0\le r,s<1\). The exact gauge \((|p+sq|+|q-rp|)/(1+rs)\) shows that \(r<s\) leaves only \(\pm e_1\) shortest and \(s<r\) only \(\pm e_2\); the source completeness criterion requires diameter segments meeting every edge, so completeness forces \(r=s\). The zero endpoint is the known incomplete diamond and every positive equal-parameter case is the published twisted-square example. The area, diameter and polar involution then follow algebraically. The inspected exact-arithmetic verifier agrees on rational stress tests; the real-parameter theorem rests on the symbolic inequalities.

originality.rationale: The defining 2024 paper was inspected through the reducedness/completeness characterizations, the twisted-square example and Question 5.3. It presents the family as examples and classifies triangles separately; it does not state the origin-symmetric quadrilateral converse. A fresh Resultary search found the audited classification as the direct exact hit and no stronger covering result. The older Bárány--Füredi paper remains a bounded historical risk: public routes exposed only abstract/bibliographic material, and the permitted institutional retrieval returned the wrong article from the same journal volume rather than the target paper.

value.rationale: The defining paper explicitly asks for structure of simultaneously lattice reduced and complete bodies and supplies twisted squares only as examples. The origin-symmetric quadrilateral case is a natural smallest polygonal classification, and the proof gives a structural reason—loss of a second diameter-direction pair—why unequal twists fail.

limitations: No classification of nonsymmetric quadrilaterals or higher-vertex polygons.
